Compact witnesses · truncation boxes · integral comparison

Improper power integrals

An improper integral needs a computation tailored to its function: justified finite integrals, lower and upper estimates, and a proved error schedule.

Checked scope: integer exponents. The results below cover both improper endpoints for integer powers and the convergence classification for natural-exponent series. The requested theorem for arbitrary represented-real \(p\), including \(0<p<1\), remains unfinished. No Mathlib real numbers are imported.

First justify each finite integral

Checked

For \(p=k+2\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), finite power factorization proves, on every rational cell \(0<a\le b\),

\[(b-a)b^{-p}\le\frac{a^{1-p}-b^{1-p}}{p-1}\le(b-a)a^{-p}.\]

These inequalities telescope across a partition. Uniform endpoint rectangles have gap \((b-a)(a^{-p}-b^{-p})/N\). Thus the independently specified integrand has arbitrarily tight bounds, and its compact integral equals the displayed formula. This is a function-specific proof using a sufficient rectangle specification.

compact_hasIntegral and compact_exact

What stage \(n\) computes

Checked

Set \(R_n=n+1\). The lower endpoint is a certified compact integral. The upper endpoint adds the explicit tail.

\[L_n=\frac{1-R_n^{1-p}}{p-1},\qquad U_n=\frac1{p-1}.\] \[0\le U_n-L_n=\frac{R_n^{1-p}}{p-1}\le\frac1{n+1}.\]

The box contains every later rational truncation. It nests and shrinks, with actual compact-integral witnesses supplied at each stage. Any represented value satisfying the same exhaustion law agrees with

\[\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\simeq\frac1{p-1},\qquad p=2,3,4,\ldots.\]

Computation, exhaustion, tail bounds, and exact identity

The endpoint at zero

Checked integer cases

A separate polynomial cell proof constructs the compact integrals of \(x^k\). Truncating at \(a_n=1/(n+1)\) gives the same rational box computation and proves

\[\int_0^1 x^k\,dx\simeq\frac1{k+1},\qquad k\in\mathbb N.\]

These are the cases \(p=-k\). Conversely, for \(p=k+2\), the integral from \(1/(n+1)\) to one is at least \(n/(k+1)\). The polynomial integral from one to \(n+1\) is at least \(n\). These lower estimates rule out finite limits on the divergent sides.

Compact monomial proofs and both divergence arguments

The critical exponent

Checked lower rectangles

For \(1/x\), use the cells \([a2^j,a2^{j+1}]\). Each lower rectangle has area \(1/2\); each upper rectangle has area one. After \(N\) cells,

\[L_N=\frac N2,\qquad U_N=N.\]

Use \(a=1\) at infinity and \(a=2^{-N}\) near zero. The finite lower areas force divergence. This argument does not claim a newly constructed compact logarithm evaluator.

Whole-cell evidence and nonexistence of finite exhaustion limits

Derive the series test

Checked for \(p\in\mathbb N\)

Writing \(S_N=\sum_{j=1}^N j^{-p}\), summing the compact cell estimates gives

\[\int_{N+1}^{M+1}x^{-p}\,dx\le S_M-S_N\le\int_N^M x^{-p}\,dx.\]

For \(p\ge2\), the executable series boxes are

\[\left[S_N,\ S_N+\frac{N^{1-p}}{p-1}\right],\qquad N=n+1.\]

At \(p=1\), \(S_{2^{2T}}\ge T\). At \(p=0\), \(S_N=N\). Therefore a valid represented sum exists exactly when \(p\ge2\), on the natural-exponent domain. Convergence is proved for the independent partial-sum program; uniqueness and invariance under changing the represented sum are also checked.

What remains for real exponents

Not yet proved

The full test needs a positive-base power computation for arbitrary valid represented-real exponents, its compact integration law, and representation invariance. The general thresholds are the targets

\[\int_0^1x^{-p}\,dx=\frac1{1-p}\quad(p<1),\qquad \int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx=\frac1{p-1}\quad(p>1).\]

The existing real-exponent zeta evaluator does not yet supply that integral bridge. These integer results also do not complete the Gaussian normalization or the Gamma and ball-volume bridges.
